title: The name he called
hookLine: Ajamila, dying and afraid, calls his son Narayana and Vishnu's messengers come; why puja begins with a call, and the bell sounds it
carry: the bell is a call: come
last: PUSHPA — THE FLOWER STANDS FOR YOUR HEART.

lines: A GOOD MAN WHO WENT WRONG.
cards: Ajamila started out as a good young man who kept every rule. Then he fell for the wrong life, left his wife, and lived for decades by cheating and stealing.

He had ten children, and he adored the youngest, a little boy named Narayana, one of Vishnu's names. At eighty-eight, Ajamila lay dying, and he saw them coming: three terrifying messengers of Death, ropes in their hands.
He panicked, and did what a frightened father does. He shouted for his little boy, playing outside. Narayana!
He wasn't praying. He was just calling his son.

teach.b: But the name he called was God's. And in the Bhagavata Purana, the moment it leaves his mouth, Vishnu's own messengers appear and stop Death's messengers cold.
They argue it out, and Vishnu's side wins: a name of God, called even by accident, even half-meant, is heard. Ajamila is released, and he spends the rest of his life in prayer.
Some families say that's one reason so many Hindu children carry God's names: every time you call them, you've called God too. Now, the bell. Its Sanskrit name is ghanta.

teach.h: GHANTA: PUJA BEGINS WITH A CALL.
teach.b: Every puja begins with a call, called avahana: inviting God to come. And the bell is the sound of that call.
Many families say a short traditional verse as they ring it, asking the gods to come and anything in the way to go.

teach.h: NOT AN ALARM CLOCK. A CALL.
teach.b: So the bell isn't an alarm clock for a sleepy God. It's a call, made by someone who trusts, like the story does, that calling is enough to be heard.
That's why it rings at the very start of puja, again through arti, and why people ring the big bell at a temple door as they walk in.
On top of many hand bells sits a little figure: Garuda, the eagle who carries Vishnu, or Nandi, Shiva's bull.
Many teachers add a second reading: the bell calls you too. By the time its long ring fades, you're here.

how: Many Hindus ring a small hand bell at the start of puja as part of inviting the deity (avahana), often saying a short traditional verse, ring it again during arti, and ring the large bell at a temple's entrance as they walk in. Many hand bells carry a figure on the handle, often Garuda for Vishnu's devotees or Nandi for Shiva's.

a brass plate that holds the lamp

s: Ajamila was saved because he had prayed perfectly all his life
he'd gone badly wrong. he only called his son's name, and it was one of God's names.
the puja bell is rung to wake God up
it's an invitation, avahana: calling God to come.
many Hindu children are named after names of God
some families say that's one reason: calling them is calling God too.

games.q: your little cousin asks why the bell rings before anything else in puja. what does today's teaching say?
o: it's a call: we invite God to come, and we trust the call is heard.
it tells the neighbors puja has started.
it scares the flies away from the sweets.
games.why: puja begins with avahana, inviting God in. the bell sounds the call, and in Ajamila's story even a half-meant call was heard.

practice: Strike a bell once, gently, or a glass with a spoon, or just imagine the sound. If you pray, let the ring be your call, and say one name you honor, Narayana, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, quietly, once. Then don't move.
Follow the sound as it thins out, until you can't tell whether you still hear it. When it's gone, notice where you are. You were called too.

wordCard.voice: Ghanta. The bell: rung at the start of puja to call God in, the sound of a call that, the story says, is always heard.

orig.note: Sanskrit ghaṇṭā: bell. Often written घंटा in Hindi.
